intro: Substitute teaching builds classroom skills that transfer straight into permanent teaching jobs. The closest of the 25 careers below is Kindergarten Teachers, Except Special Education, with a 94% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $62,680, which is 50% more than the $41,670 substitutes earn.
why_it_works: Walking into a new class each day means reading students fast, giving clear instructions and keeping a plan on track. O*NET rates social perceptiveness at 3.5 and instructing at 3.38 out of 5 for substitutes. That is why full-time teaching roles from kindergarten to high school are the top matches. Most need a teaching license rather than another degree, and the skills to grow are evaluation and planning.
tips: Ask the schools where you sub most often about long-term assignments; they often lead to permanent offers.
Check your state's alternative certification route if you have a bachelor's degree but no teaching license.
Special education is in demand: secondary special education teachers earn $74,260, or 78% more.

faq.q: What jobs can former substitute teachers do?
faq.a: The closest matches are kindergarten teachers (94%), elementary school teachers (93%) and secondary school teachers (92%), based on O*NET 31.0. Secondary special education teachers are also 92% matched and earn a median of $74,260, which is 78% more than substitutes earn.

faq.q: Which careers for substitute teachers pay more?
faq.a: 21 of the 25 matches pay more than the $41,670 substitute median. Postsecondary English teachers earn $78,760 (89% more), Instructional Coordinators $77,440 (86% more) and postsecondary family and consumer sciences teachers $75,870 (82% more), according to BLS May 2025 data.

faq.q: Do substitute teachers need another degree?
faq.a: For most paths, no. 20 of the 25 matches need no more education than substitutes already have, though many need a state teaching license. 5 of the 25, mostly college teaching and instructional coordination roles, usually need a graduate degree, so check before you apply.

faq.q: What skills should substitute teachers build?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are systems evaluation, judgment and decision making, coordination and managing materials. Time management already rates 3.12 out of 5 in O*NET for substitutes, so planning a full year of lessons is the main new step.
